entities.name: Ayyubid dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Ayyubid dynasty (1171–1260 CE) was a Sunni Muslim dynasty founded by the Kurdish military commander Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub). Ruling Egypt, Syria, the Jazira, Yemen, and parts of Arabia and North Africa, the Ayyubids are celebrated primarily for Saladin's reconquest of Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187 — one of the most significant military events of the medieval era.

Saladin's 1187 defeat of the Crusader Kingdom at the Battle of Hattin and subsequent recapture of Jerusalem (lost to the First Crusade in 1099) shocked Christendom and prompted the Third Crusade. His chivalrous treatment of Jerusalem's Christian inhabitants — refusing the massacre that had accompanied the 1099 conquest — earned him respect from both Muslim and Christian sources, including admiration from his adversary Richard I of England.

The Ayyubid dynasty fostered trade between the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean, maintained Cairo as a center of Islamic learning, and patronized architecture including the Cairo Citadel. The Ayyubid administrative system — using a confederation of Kurdish and Turkish commanders governing subdivided territories — eventually led to the rise of Mamluk military slaves who overthrew the dynasty in 1250, with the Mongol Hulagu Khan's western campaigns completing the dynasty's fragmentation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty reconquered Jerusalem and demonstrated that Islamic civilization could match Crusader military power, becoming the defining symbol of Muslim resistance to European holy war.
